doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Dream gigs: New York Philharmonic, Steely Dan, classic multitracks
summary: Asked about hypothetical calls, he would try the Philharmonic and love touring with Steely Dan, and wishes to hear multitracks of Motown, Beatles and other classics, with reverb baked in.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Let me suggest two things that if they ever happen to you — what would be the first thing that would come to your mind? So your phone rings and someone asks would you live mix the New York Philharmonic in Central Park? What’s the first thing that comes to your mind?

Wow that’s scary. I’d love to do it but it’s a very big undertaking you know. And there are a fair number of people who will be in the audience, you know 150,000 people all figured it should be sounding somewhere — sounding differently. It would be, I suppose I’d like to try it. A tiny bit out of my wheelhouse but I would still like to try it.
How about if you got a call to do a four month tour as a live mixer for Steely Dan?
Oh well yeah. That — I’d be all over that. I’d have to talk to my buddy Coach [Michael Conner] who is their live front house guy. Yeah.
You could switch chairs with him, put him on SNL.

Yeah he’d be fine. We worked together when Paul Simon was through the show. Yeah that would be quite the challenge, that would be quite the amazing thing to do. You know and it’s funny people, and I think rightly so, look at some of those Steely Dan records as just sort of the pinnacle, like the urrtex of how you create a pop record. But there are also just other — and the same way some people I would love to hear like these original multi-tracks from the Beatles stuff and so forth — well sure, who wouldn’t? But then there are certain Motown songs, or certain classic California sound stuff like from The Association or things from The Spinners, some of that Philadelphia stuff. I would love to see what those multi-tracks sound like. Or some early Elton John or Jethro Tull, things like that. I’d just love to hear how that all sounds and get a sense of what those balances are. Because it’s really about just finding space for everything in the mix and how it’s just all going to sit. And I guess the other thing would be when those things were being recorded the assumption is — to hearken back to what I said earlier — is that they were thinking about the mix. But to know what the end mix sounds like now and to then hear the raw elements and think about wow how did they get there and how much is baked into the tracks. Because sometimes you would put a lot of reverb on and so forth. Now, if you don’t need to commit to anything people just don’t. Because everything is digital. That is all plug-ins if you’re working in Pro Tools you add reverb after the fact, all of this stuff, but a lot of Beatles and a lot of other records of the day, certain reverb and echo delays and so forth were baked into the tracks. And you made those decisions then and there. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
